A strangeness ran through all this which drew and enchanted me. He seemed at last to have awakened from his prolonged, visionary slumber, feeling something like one of the seven sleepers, or Nourjahad in that charming imitation of an Eastern story. Diana had vanished; his friends were altered or dead; and, upon this awakening, I was all that remained for him to love in the world.

How precious to me were Loch Lomond’s waters, mountains, and woods, now that my wanderings were shared by a companion so beloved. With my father I sought out every delightful place, on the islands or beside the waterfalls sheltered by trees, along each shaded path or through hollows tangled with fern and brushwood. His conversation widened my thoughts. I felt made anew, surrounded by the freshness and vitality of a new creature, as though his arrival had borne me from a confined corner of earth into a universe without bounds for either understanding or imagination. Until then my life had resembled a pleasant country brook, fated never to stray from its native meadows, but to sink quietly away when its course was finished and leave no sign. Now I thought it a varied river, running through a fertile, beautiful landscape, always altering and always lovely. Alas, I knew nothing of the desert toward which it flowed, the rocks that would rend its waters, or the ghastly prospect that its waves would mirror in still greater distortion. Life shone brightly then; I was learning to hope, and what despair strikes the heart more bitterly than the destruction of hope?

How strange that sorrow should tread so closely upon happiness so divine! I drank from an enchanted cup, yet gall lay beneath its lingering sweetness. My heart overflowed with profound affection, and its very fullness and depth gave it peace. I did not conceive that love might produce misery; that lesson, which everyone must learn at last, came to me in a form few are compelled to suffer. I mourn now, and must always mourn, those brief months of paradisal bliss. I violated no command, tasted no apple, and nevertheless was mercilessly expelled. Alas, my companion did, and I was carried headlong in his fall. But I stray from my account—let sorrow arrive at its appointed hour; at this point in my story I may still dwell upon happiness.

Three months went by in this delightful companionship before my aunt became ill. I spent an entire month nursing her in her chamber, but the illness was fatal, and she died, leaving me inconsolable for a time. How terrible death is to the living! Habit forges such strong chains, even where affection does not join their links, that their breaking must bring agony to the heart.

He sprang up and grabbed her arm roughly. “Show him to me. Which one is he? Point him out. I have to see him!” he cried. But just then the Duke of Berwick’s four-horse carriage passed between them and the other carriage. By the time the view was clear again, it had swept out of the park.

“He’s gone,” Sibyl murmured sadly. “I wish you’d seen him.”

“So do I. Because, as surely as there is a God in heaven, if he ever hurts you, I’ll kill him.”

She stared at him in horror. He said it again, his words slicing through the air like a knife. People around them began to stare. A woman standing beside her gave a little giggle.

“Come away, Jim. Come away,” she whispered. He followed stubbornly as she made her way through the crowd. He was glad he had said it.

At the Achilles Statue she turned to face him. The pity in her eyes became laughter on her lips, and she shook her head. “You’re foolish, Jim, utterly foolish—just a bad-tempered boy. How can you say such terrible things? You don’t know what you’re talking about. You’re simply jealous and unkind. Oh, I wish you would fall in love. Love makes people good, and what you said was wicked.”

“I’m sixteen,” he replied, “and I know what I’m doing. Mother is no help to you. She doesn’t know how to take care of you. Now I wish I weren’t going to Australia at all. I’m very tempted to give the whole thing up. I would, if I hadn’t signed my contract.”

“Oh, don’t be so solemn, Jim. You sound like a hero from one of those silly melodramas Mother used to love acting in. I won’t argue with you. I’ve seen him, and oh, seeing him is perfect happiness. We mustn’t quarrel. I know you’d never hurt anyone I love, would you?”

“Not while you love him, I suppose,” he answered sullenly.

“I’ll love him forever!” she cried.

“And him?”

“Forever too!”

“He’d better.”

She drew back from him. Then she laughed and laid her hand on his arm. He was only a boy.

They hailed an omnibus at Marble Arch, and it dropped them near their shabby home on Euston Road. It was past five, and Sibyl needed to lie down for a couple of hours before her performance. Jim insisted that she do so. He said he would rather say goodbye when their mother wasn’t there. She was certain to make a scene, and he hated scenes of every kind.

The flickering gas lamps curved away into the distance. Outside a small house enclosed by walls stood a single horse-drawn cab, its driver asleep inside. He hurried toward Portland Place, glancing back from time to time as though afraid someone was following him. At the corner of Rich Street, two men were reading a small notice on a wooden fence. A strange curiosity drew him across the road. As he approached, he saw the word “Murder” in black letters. He flinched, and his cheek flushed deeply. The notice offered a reward for information leading to the arrest of a man of medium height, aged between thirty and forty, wearing a bowler hat, black coat, and checked trousers, with a scar on his right cheek. He read it again and again, wondering whether the unfortunate man would be caught and how he had got his scar. Perhaps one day his own name would be posted on walls across London. Perhaps a reward would be offered for him too.

The thought made him feel sick with horror. He spun around and hurried into the night.

He barely knew where he went. He dimly remembered wandering through a maze of shabby houses and losing himself in a vast web of dark streets. Bright daylight was breaking when he finally reached Piccadilly Circus. Walking home toward Belgrave Square, he passed the great wagons heading for Covent Garden. The drivers, wearing white smocks, had friendly, sunburned faces and coarse, curly hair. They strode along strongly, cracking their whips and occasionally calling to one another. A plump boy rode a huge gray horse at the head of a team whose harness jingled. Primroses were tucked into his battered hat, and he laughed as his small hands held tightly to the horse’s mane. The high heaps of vegetables looked like masses of jade against the morning sky—green jade set against the pink petals of some wonderful rose. Lord Arthur felt strangely moved, though he could not explain why. The delicate beauty of the dawn seemed unbearably sad to him. He thought of all the days that begin in beauty and end in storms. And these country people, with their rough, cheerful voices and easygoing manners—what a strange version of London they saw! A London without the sins of night or the smoke of day: a pale, ghostly city, a deserted town of tombs. He wondered what they thought of it. Did they know anything of its magnificence and disgrace, its fierce, fiery pleasures and its terrible hunger, or all that it created and ruined between morning and evening?
